content:
Hold on until the last moment

"To be honest, I held on until the last moment." The two sisters grew up at Wang Fuk Court with their parents. Their father later passed away and the elder sister got married, so Miss Yuen lived with her mother alone until the fire. Her mother perished in the blaze. During the past period of going upstairs, she once wore a sweater with the handwritten slogan "rebuild on the original site" to voice her demand. But the authorities rejected the proposal and the owners' corporation refused to discuss it. It was only one week before the 31 August acquisition deadline that she submitted a "letter accepting the acquisition proposal".

Miss Yuen believes the residents of Wang Fuk Court have already been "crushed like a crab under a boulder". She says the two explainers she had contacted were unable to answer her questions; they only had one clear objective, which was to press neighbours about whether they had sold their flats.

Post-disaster life feels like 'just staying over'

Since the fire, Miss Yuen has stayed at Shin Lau in Tai Po and later moved to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a "temporary residence fee" every month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet that had been in the unit, as well as the neighbours and the security guard, all keep reminding her of her status. She describes her life after the incident as "just staying over".

Rethinking what counts as 'home' and what counts as 'a house'?

Every day after work, she returns to this empty unit at eight or nine o'clock, and on holidays she chooses to leave and go to her sister's home. "Since the incident, I've started thinking about what 'home' means, what 'a house' means. A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when the home that is Wang Fuk Court can still be burned down by someone..."

The word 'home' has become quite heavy for me

When the reporter asked Miss Yuen about her imagination of home, she said the old phone containing photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories exist only in her mind. She sighed deeply and said, "A home is not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, a full set of home appliances that make it a so-called proper home. It made me rethink what the elements of a proper home are, so I can't answer this question yet, because the word 'home' has become quite heavy for me now."

Dissatisfied with officials' 'letting go' remarks

The responses of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire—such as Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing's remarks about 'letting go' and Financial Secretary Deputy John Wong's talk of market value—have only added to her helplessness and anger. "The more you stay silent, the less I can understand." "When they can actually say something so cold and detached, what exactly do they think the meaning of home is?"

A sense of 'selling at a knockdown price'

Miss Yuen recalled that the strongest feeling at the moment she signed the letter accepting the acquisition was a sense of unwillingness and "indignation"—a sense of being "sold off cheap"—because a home is not only its material value but also its ties to emotions and memories. "The flat was something my dad and mum worked so hard for. If it is really taken from me for nothing like that, I would actually feel even more unreconciled than the feeling of being 'sold cheap' now."

After signing the letter, Miss Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has postponed submitting its report until October. Miss Yuen says pursuing accountability is one part of it, "but how a person is supposed to move on, I can't answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss—first, the home was burned down, and what that burning down means is that it feels as if the history of my growing up has been wiped away. A family member also passed away in the fire, and suddenly at that. ... There is a big hole in my heart, and whether that hole can really be filled, or whether one day it can heal—I don't know how to answer that."
